power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Consumer decision-making unfolds through a complex sequence of interactions across multiple touchpoints and channels.
The rapid proliferation of generative AI (Gen-AI) represents a fundamental shift in this process, reshaping what information consumers encounter and how much cognitive effort they expend.
Rather than actively navigating a series of discrete exposures to information, Gen-AI systems provide aggregated search results, synthesized comparisons, and annotated recommendations.

By March 2026, 68% of consumers reported incorporating Gen-AIenabled search for product decisions (Adams et al., 2026), with a substantial portion trusting AI recommendations more than paid search results (Dooley, 2025).
text.formatted: By March 2026, 68% of consumers reported incorporating Gen-AIenabled search for product decisions <ref type="bibr">(Adams et al., 2026)</ref>, with a substantial portion trusting AI recommendations more than paid search results <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dooley, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The cognitive processes of making a decision are no longer confined within the consumer, but are distributed across human-AI interactions, with Gen-AI performing portions of the evaluative process.

As product search, comparison, and evaluation are increasingly conducted by AI, advertising designed to influence consumer cognition directly, such as search and display advertising, lose effectiveness if consumers are no longer performing the cognitive work those formats presume.

These developments challenge a foundational, but largely implicit, assumption in advertising theory that the consumer is the primary locus of brand evaluation, and that advertising exerts its effects by shaping processing within that internal system.
This assumption, of course, was always a bounded approximation. Simon (1955) established that cognitive capacity is limited and decisions are made with sufficient rather than optimal information.
text.formatted: This assumption, of course, was always a bounded approximation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Simon (1955)</ref> established that cognitive capacity is limited and decisions are made with sufficient rather than optimal information.

text.text: Advertising theory absorbed this insight at what Marr (1982) describes as the computational level, accommodating low-elaboration consumers through peripheral routes and heuristic cues, but left intact a deeper, unexamined commitment to the individual as the site of implementation for the cognitive processes underlying persuasion.
text.formatted: Advertising theory absorbed this insight at what <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Marr (1982)</ref> describes as the computational level, accommodating low-elaboration consumers through peripheral routes and heuristic cues, but left intact a deeper, unexamined commitment to the individual as the site of implementation for the cognitive processes underlying persuasion.

text.text: This commitment is evident across theories such as the Elaboration Likelihood Model, the Persuasion Knowledge Model, and hierarchy-of-effects frameworks.
Although these theories specify the goals and conditions of persuasion, they do not explicitly address where the underlying cognitive work occurs.
Implicitly, they share an implementationlevel assumption that evaluation, elaboration, and attitude formation take place within the individual consumer's biological mind.

It is true that prior technologies have enabled consumers to externalize portions of their cognitive processes (e.g., Google search, Yelp, recommendation systems), but these processes are constrained enough in scope that bounded-cognition assumptions remain workable.

Gen-AI renders that assumption untenable by expanding the scope and form of that delegation, from information retrieval to automated action, the stages of consumers' decision-making that were previously less susceptible to externalization.

When different stages of decision processes are delegated to Gen-AI, the locus of learning, persuasion, and brand influence becomes increasingly distributed across human-technology systems rather than residing fully within the consumer.

Cognitive science has long recognized that cognition extends across tools, artifacts, and environments through cognitive offloading, the use of external resources to reduce internal cognitive demands (Clark & Chalmers, 1998; Risko & Gilbert, 2016).
text.formatted: Cognitive science has long recognized that cognition extends across tools, artifacts, and environments through cognitive offloading, the use of external resources to reduce internal cognitive demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Clark & Chalmers, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Risko & Gilbert, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: While cognitive offloading has long been examined in cognitive psychology, prior work largely focused on learning and memory outcomes (Gilbert, 2015; Ferguson et al., 2015).
text.formatted: While cognitive offloading has long been examined in cognitive psychology, prior work largely focused on learning and memory outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gilbert, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ferguson et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Less research has addressed how cognitive offloading reshapes the consumer decision process beyond information acquisition to later stages, such as information integration, comparison of alternatives, evaluation, and choice, particularly as Gen-AI increasingly supports these functions (Clark, 2025).
text.formatted: Less research has addressed how cognitive offloading reshapes the consumer decision process beyond information acquisition to later stages, such as information integration, comparison of alternatives, evaluation, and choice, particularly as Gen-AI increasingly supports these functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Clark, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For advertising, consumers' cognitive offloading to Gen-AI implies a fundamental reallocation of cognitive labor and decision control from consumers to Gen-AI, with downstream consequences for brand learning, persuasion, loyalty formation, and consumer agency.

This paper proposes a theoretical framework for understanding when consumers cognitively offload one or multiple decision processes to Gen-AI and articulates the cognitive and persuasive outcomes of such offloading decisions.
First, we introduce a delegation continuum that maps the stages of the consumer decision process along which cognitive work can be distributed between the consumer and Gen-AI.
Drawing on cognitive offloading research and value-based decision principles (Gilbert, 2024), we then categorize and contextualize key antecedents that predict offloading.

text.text: Metacognitive beliefs, individual traits, and performance goals moderate these cost-benefit perceptions.
Building on this foundation, the paper further examines outcomes of cognitive offloading to Gen-AI systems.

We show how cognitive offloading produces memory trade-offs, metacognitive illusions, verification costs, and longer-term shifts in consumer autonomy and brand loyalty, developing seven propositions and three conjectures.
We conclude by outlining interventions that may recalibrate reliance on Gen-AI while preserving consumer agency.

Taken together, this work shifts advertising research from messages and exposures to the distribution of cognition in human-AI systems, providing a new perspective for understanding advertising in an era of AI-mediated choice.
This paper first employs theory adaptation (Jaakkola, 2020), a conceptual design in which one form of adaptation involves shifting the level of analysis.

text.text: To specify the level being shifted and situate cognitive offloading within advertising theory, we draw on Marr's (1982) tri-level framework.
text.formatted: To specify the level being shifted and situate cognitive offloading within advertising theory, we draw on <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Marr's (1982)</ref> tri-level framework.

text.text: This framework distinguishes three analytically separate questions about any information-processing system: the computational level (what goal does it serve), the algorithmic level (how that goal is achieved), and the implementation level (where those processes occur; Huskey et al., 2020; Marr, 1982).
text.formatted: This framework distinguishes three analytically separate questions about any information-processing system: the computational level (what goal does it serve), the algorithmic level (how that goal is achieved), and the implementation level (where those processes occur; <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Huskey et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Marr, 1982</ref>).

text.text: Marr's framework was originally developed in the field of vision science, but the analytic power of the framework applies broadly to information-processing systems.
This includes consumer cognitions that advertising theory has long sought to describe.
By this distinction, most advertising and communication theories operate primarily at the computational level.

They specify the goals of persuasion (e.g., attitude change) and the conditions under which persuasion succeeds, but not how those processes are carried out or where they take place (Huskey et al., 2020).
text.formatted: They specify the goals of persuasion (e.g., attitude change) and the conditions under which persuasion succeeds, but not how those processes are carried out or where they take place <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Huskey et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) posits that motivation and ability determine the processing route (Petty et al., 2005), but it does not specify how it transitions between processing routes, or what mechanisms produce elaboration, nor does it address whether these processes must occur entirely within the individual.

text.text: The Persuasion Knowledge Model (Friestad & Wright, 1994), hierarchy-of-effects models (Lavidge & Steiner, 1961), and brand learning theories (Alba & Hutchinson, 2000) all similarly exemplify this emphasis.
text.formatted: The Persuasion Knowledge Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Friestad & Wright, 1994)</ref>, hierarchy-of-effects models <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Lavidge & Steiner, 1961)</ref>, and brand learning theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alba & Hutchinson, 2000)</ref> all similarly exemplify this emphasis.

text.text: Consequently, advertising theory leaves open the question of how evaluative processing is executed and where it is located-a question that becomes increasingly important as emerging technologies enable parts of this processing to occur outside the individual.
What each of these frameworks shares implicitly is an assumption at the implementation (physical system) level: that the cognitive work occurs within the individual consumer's biological mind.
This assumption has been so foundational as to go unstated: persuasion, in the dominant tradition, is mediated by internal cognitive elaboration.

The LC4MP (Lang, 2006; Fisher et al., 2018a, b) introduces a breakdown of this logic: when message demands exceed the consumer's finite cognitive resources, individuals may turn to cognitive offloading to relieve themselves of the demands of the cognitive task.
text.formatted: The LC4MP <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Lang, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fisher et al., 2018a, b)</ref> introduces a breakdown of this logic: when message demands exceed the consumer's finite cognitive resources, individuals may turn to cognitive offloading to relieve themselves of the demands of the cognitive task.

text.text: Yet, advertising research has assumed adjustment occurs internally through heuristic processing, reduced elaboration, or disengagement.

These advertising theories have yet to consider the possibility that cognitive processes or evaluative labor can be redistributed to an external system, and that one's biological mind is not the only physical system in which those processes can be implemented.
Cognitive science offers a concept, cognitive offloading, that connects the computational accounts of persuasion with the implementation-level question of where that cognitive work is realized.

In information-rich environments replete with external support, cognitive offloading allows users to bypass cognitive limitations (e.g., working memory constraints, limited attention) and avoid cognitive overload by delegating parts of processing to external resources.

From this perspective, frameworks such as ELM, PKM, the Hierarchy of Effects model, and brand learning theories specify computational-level goals that can, in principle, be achieved across distributed cognitive systems.

Rather than replacing existing advertising theories, cognitive offloading therefore identifies the implementation-level assumption on which they depend and specifies where that assumption progressively breaks down.
Humans have long recruited external resources to reduce cognitive demands.
The practice of cognitive offloading can be traced back to antiquity (e.g., systems of knots or quipus for memory, Nestojko et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The practice of cognitive offloading can be traced back to antiquity (e.g., systems of knots or quipus for memory, <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Nestojko et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Examples include using language, mathematical notation, and depictive representations like maps and diagrams, which enhance human reasoning and reduce the burden on internal memory (Clark & Chalmers, 1998).
text.formatted: Examples include using language, mathematical notation, and depictive representations like maps and diagrams, which enhance human reasoning and reduce the burden on internal memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Clark & Chalmers, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Transactive memory theory formalizes this insight at the social level: individuals in relationships and groups retrieve information through other people, which effectively distributes cognition across a social system (Wegner, 1987).
text.formatted: Transactive memory theory formalizes this insight at the social level: individuals in relationships and groups retrieve information through other people, which effectively distributes cognition across a social system <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Wegner, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: In contemporary contexts, cognitive offloading also extends across digital technologies (Hamilton & Benjamin, 2019), where individuals use devices as repositories of representational information, such as using search engines to retrieve information (Sparrow et al., 2011).
text.formatted: In contemporary contexts, cognitive offloading also extends across digital technologies <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hamilton & Benjamin, 2019)</ref>, where individuals use devices as repositories of representational information, such as using search engines to retrieve information <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Sparrow et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these tools allows individuals to offload a bounded cognitive task, shifting a portion of the decision process from the biological mind to external systems, while consumers are still responsible for integrating outputs and making judgments.
Fully internal cognition was, as Simon (1955) established, always a bounded approximation.
text.formatted: Fully internal cognition was, as <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Simon (1955)</ref> established, always a bounded approximation.

text.text: Therefore, the question is not "whether consumers offload," but how much of the decision process can be delegated, and what kinds of cognitive work are transferred.

Because of this, we propose a delegation continuum for consumer decision-making that maps the progression of cognitive offloading across the stages of product search and evaluation, from its most bounded form to its most expansive, organized by the type of cognitive work being transferred.
We draw on Parasuraman et al.'s (2000) function-based taxonomy of human-machine automation.
text.formatted: We draw on <ref type="bibr">Parasuraman et al.'s (2000)</ref> function-based taxonomy of human-machine automation.

text.text: This taxonomy distinguishes information acquisition, information analysis, decision selection, and action implementation across ten levels of automation ranging from Level 1 (fully manual: the human performs all work) to Level 10 (fully autonomous: the system acts without human involvement).
We adapt this framework to consumer decision-making by proposing a seven-stage delegation continuum.
The delegation continuum for consumer decision-making maps onto these function types with increasing automation levels.
Stages 1 and 2 (information retrieval and synthesis) correspond to information acquisition at lower automation levels.
At Stage 1 (storage/retrieval), consumers query apps for items, prices, and specifications.
At Stage 2 (synthesis), systems such as Yelp integrate and summarize information across sources.
Stages 3-4 (comparison and evaluation) correspond to information analysis and early decision selection.
At Stage 3 (comparison), websites like Amazon present options side by side on specified attributes.
At Stage 4, alternative evaluation occurs when a feature-matching algorithm evaluates products against stated preferences, effectively performing the comparative judgment on the consumer's behalf.
At Stage 5 (recommendation), systems such as Netflix or Spotify rank and surface options tailored to inferred preferences.
Stages 6-7 (decision execution and automated action) correspond to action implementation at high automation levels.

Stage 6 executes a decision without requiring consumers' approval per step, and Stage 7, like the agentic system, monitors, decides, and acts on predetermined rules without any further engagement from consumers, approaching full automation as described in Parasuraman et al.

Each stage of offloading can be performed by a technological feature, but none of these technologies has the capacity to span the full range, leaving consumers responsible for integrating outputs across stages (Table 1).
text.formatted: Each stage of offloading can be performed by a technological feature, but none of these technologies has the capacity to span the full range, leaving consumers responsible for integrating outputs across stages (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Gen-AI breaks this pattern by occupying all the stages across this delegation continuum.

With a single prompt that describes their needs, consumers can receive a synthesized overview, a comparison of products, ranked recommendations, and can even proceed with making decisions and executing transactions using an agentic AI.
While prior technologies cover one or several stages of the decision-making process, the integrative and evaluative work still largely remains 1 There are meaningful variations within a stage.

Two technologies that both perform recommendation may differ substantially in how much evaluative labor remains with the consumer: a traditional recommender system outputs a ranked list of options based on behavioral patterns, leaving the consumer to evaluate which recommendation to act on, while a generative AI system delivers a synthesized evaluative recommendation with explicit reasoningsubstantially reducing the evaluative work that remains internal.
The delegation continuum therefore operates simultaneously across stages -by type of cognitive function -and within each stage -by degree of automation.
with consumers.
Comparatively, Gen-AI produces a qualitative shift: it can absorb all cognitive work and eliminate the cognitive integration that previously occurred between decision stages.
In classic offloading, individuals are typically aware of what they are delegating.

Unlike earlier forms of offloading, Gen-AI also creates the possibility of a cognitive illusion of agency, whereby consumers experience themselves as making evaluative judgments that were largely performed externally.
This possibility motivates the metacognitive outcomes developed later in the paper.

As users delegate higher-order cognitive processes to AI, Gen-AI chatbots transform from passive repositories of information into active extended-cognition partners (Orrù et al., 2023; Urban et al., 2024).

text.text: When Do We Offload?

Outlining Antecedents for Advertising Research Gilbert (2024) formalizes cognitive offloading as a value-based decision process in which individuals delegate cognitive work to an external source when the expected utility of offloading exceeds that of internal processing.
text.formatted: Outlining Antecedents for Advertising Research <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Gilbert (2024)</ref> formalizes cognitive offloading as a value-based decision process in which individuals delegate cognitive work to an external source when the expected utility of offloading exceeds that of internal processing.

text.text: Applied to consumer decision making, delegating product search and evaluation to generative AI reflects a comparative assessment of the relative costs and benefits of internal processing (by the consumer) versus external processing (by AI systems).

Offloading becomes more likely as the costs of internal processing increase due to situational demands or individual cognitive constraints associated with complex tasks (Risko et al., 2014), and as the benefits of external processing increase, such as improved decision quality and reduced cognitive effort (Gao & Garagnani, 2025; Grinschgl et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Offloading becomes more likely as the costs of internal processing increase due to situational demands or individual cognitive constraints associated with complex tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Risko et al., 2014)</ref>, and as the benefits of external processing increase, such as improved decision quality and reduced cognitive effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gao & Garagnani, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Grinschgl et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, offloading is less likely when the costs of external processing rise, including low reliability and usability and increased post-offloading costs (e.g., verification costs), or when the benefits of internal processing are salient, such as preserving autonomy and cultivating expertise (Hamilton & Benjamin, 2019).
text.formatted: Conversely, offloading is less likely when the costs of external processing rise, including low reliability and usability and increased post-offloading costs (e.g., verification costs), or when the benefits of internal processing are salient, such as preserving autonomy and cultivating expertise <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hamilton & Benjamin, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these determinants are not independent categories but reflect positions along a shared value continuum such that a reduction in cost can simultaneously function as a gain in benefit, and vice versa.
We use this value-based framework to organize key categories of variables that are especially relevant to advertising researchers investigating Gen-AI-mediated consumer decision-making.
Internal processing costs arise from task demands and individual cognitive constraints that increase the effort, difficulty, or likelihood of error in unaided decision making.

Task complexity stands out as a central factor that increases the cost of internal processing, as it increases both the number of elements that must be considered (e.g., brands, attributes, information sources; Hu et al., 2007; Hærem et al., 2015) and the need to integrate those elements and evaluate trade-offs (Wood, 1986; Hærem et al., 2015).

text.text: Greater task complexity creates greater demands for sustained attention, which increases the likelihood of offloading to algorithms (Wahn et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Greater task complexity creates greater demands for sustained attention, which increases the likelihood of offloading to algorithms <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Wahn et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Multitasking further elevates costs by introducing additional cognitive load (Gilbert et al., 2015; Grinschgl et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Multitasking further elevates costs by introducing additional cognitive load <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gilbert et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Grinschgl et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, individual cognitive constraints, such as short-term memory (STM), working memory limitations, and age-related decline, further increase the offloading likelihood when external systems offer superior reasoning capacity (Richmond & Taylor, 2025; Risko & Dunn, 2015).
text.formatted: Finally, individual cognitive constraints, such as short-term memory (STM), working memory limitations, and age-related decline, further increase the offloading likelihood when external systems offer superior reasoning capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Richmond & Taylor, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Risko & Dunn, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The benefits of external processing reflect the performance and efficiency gains that make cognitive offloading an attractive alternative to internal processing.

Past research identifies performance advantages, particularly improvements in accuracy and reliability, as a central benefit of processing externally (Risko & Dunn, 2015; Gilbert, 2024; Gao & Garagnani, 2025).
text.formatted: Past research identifies performance advantages, particularly improvements in accuracy and reliability, as a central benefit of processing externally <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Risko & Dunn, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Gilbert, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Gao & Garagnani, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: When individuals offload to external aids, information is retained more reliably than in memory alone (Gilbert et al., 2020; Grinschgl et al., 2023; Weis & Wiese, 2019).
text.formatted: When individuals offload to external aids, information is retained more reliably than in memory alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gilbert et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Grinschgl et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Weis & Wiese, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Offloading also provides cognitive resource liberation: when consumers offload one task to Gen-AI, it reduces opportunity costs and frees limited attentional and working memory resources for other concurrent tasks (Grinschgl et al., 2023; Storm & Stone, 2015).
text.formatted: Offloading also provides cognitive resource liberation: when consumers offload one task to Gen-AI, it reduces opportunity costs and frees limited attentional and working memory resources for other concurrent tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Grinschgl et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Storm & Stone, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Accessibility further amplifies these benefits.
When external cognitive aids are readily available, easily accessible, and simple to use, individuals are more likely to rely on them (Clark & Chalmers, 1998; Clark, 2005).
text.formatted: When external cognitive aids are readily available, easily accessible, and simple to use, individuals are more likely to rely on them <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Clark & Chalmers, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Clark, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Gen-AI's accessibility via multiple devices with conversational interfaces makes it especially attractive as a cognitive offloading tool, valued for improving decision quality and reducing cognitive fatigue.
Factors that increase the costs of external processing fall into two broad categories: tool reliability and usability, and post-offload costs.

Poor tool reliability and usability, such as delays, malfunctions, and the physical and cognitive actions required to access, set up, and input requests, impose temporal and interaction costs, which have been found to reduce offloading behavior (Grinschgl et al., 2021 (Grinschgl et al., , 2023;; Gilbert, 2015; Weis & Wiese, 2019; Storm & Stone, 2015).
text.formatted: Poor tool reliability and usability, such as delays, malfunctions, and the physical and cognitive actions required to access, set up, and input requests, impose temporal and interaction costs, which have been found to reduce offloading behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Grinschgl et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Grinschgl et al., , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Gilbert, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Weis & Wiese, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Storm & Stone, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: When an external cognitive aid produces unreliable or opaque outputs, additional post-offloading costs arise (Storm & Stone, 2015).
text.formatted: When an external cognitive aid produces unreliable or opaque outputs, additional post-offloading costs arise <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Storm & Stone, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For Gen-AI, the most salient include rework costs, verification costs, and liability costs.

When AI produces biased results or hallucinations, consumers need to repeat the request (Castillo et al., 2021), verify using additional sources (Dimitriadis et al., 2024), and experience emotional and responsibility burdens (Hohenstein & Jung, 2020).
text.formatted: When AI produces biased results or hallucinations, consumers need to repeat the request <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Castillo et al., 2021)</ref>, verify using additional sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dimitriadis et al., 2024)</ref>, and experience emotional and responsibility burdens <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Hohenstein & Jung, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Internal processing can foster long-term benefits through "desirable difficulties," helping users develop schemas and expertise and preserve autonomy and satisfaction.

Consumers who expect future purchases in the same category prefer more effortful and elaborate processing to develop schemas for the category, which help them to form more efficient and informed choices in the future (Vogrincic-Haselbacher et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Consumers who expect future purchases in the same category prefer more effortful and elaborate processing to develop schemas for the category, which help them to form more efficient and informed choices in the future <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Vogrincic-Haselbacher et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In the long term, relying on internal processing is critical for the cultivation of expertise (Hamilton & Benjamin, 2019).
text.formatted: In the long term, relying on internal processing is critical for the cultivation of expertise <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hamilton & Benjamin, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Internal processing also satisfies needs for autonomy, competence, and self-expression, particularly for high-involvement or identityrelevant categories.

These benefits are largely long-term, fostering skill development and identity formation, which suggests that resistance to offloading reflects not only cognitive constraints but also motivational and identity-based considerations.
Ultimately, a consumer's decision to offload depends on their evaluation of themselves, their goals, and their environment.
Therefore, individual factors and goals moderate offload decisions by influencing how costs and benefits are perceived, weighted, and traded off against one another.
Moderators do not themselves create cognitive costs or processing benefits, but they shape decision-makers' sensitivity to existing costs and benefits.

Below we provide a brief overview of the most distinctive moderators that shape a consumer's perception of their information environment: metacognitive biases, individual traits, performance goals, and situational factors.
Metacognitive beliefs emerge as one of the strongest moderators influencing how individuals perceive their cognitive abilities, tasks, and tools.
Metacognition refers to higher-order thinking, or "thinking about thinking," that underlies evaluation or control of one's mental processes (Risko & Gilbert, 2016).
text.formatted: Metacognition refers to higher-order thinking, or "thinking about thinking," that underlies evaluation or control of one's mental processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Risko & Gilbert, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Erroneous metacognitive evaluations modify one's offloading behavior.

Research on metacognitive bias related to cognitive abilities suggests that users are imperfectly calibrated in assessing their own performance; such miscalibration increases perceived internal processing costs and promotes offloading (Gilbert et al., 2020; Rummel et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Research on metacognitive bias related to cognitive abilities suggests that users are imperfectly calibrated in assessing their own performance; such miscalibration increases perceived internal processing costs and promotes offloading <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gilbert et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Rummel et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals also exhibit metacognitive biases regarding task demands (Dunn, Lutes, & Risko, 2016; Dunn, Gaspar, & Risko, 2019; Dunn & Risko, 2016), avoiding conditions perceived as harder.
text.formatted: Individuals also exhibit metacognitive biases regarding task demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Dunn, Lutes, & Risko, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Dunn, Gaspar, & Risko, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Dunn & Risko, 2016)</ref>, avoiding conditions perceived as harder.

text.text: Research on metacognitive biases related to tools suggests that users are systematically biased to believe that using external tools is more reliable and efficient (Virgo et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Research on metacognitive biases related to tools suggests that users are systematically biased to believe that using external tools is more reliable and efficient <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Virgo et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This bias is conceptually similar to research on automation bias (Lyell & Coiera, 2017) and machine heuristics (Sundar & Kim, 2019), which increase the perceived benefits of external processing, thereby increasing the likelihood of offloading.

text.text: Individual traits, preferences, and past experiences stand out as another group of moderators.

Individual traits, such as high need for cognition (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982) and analytical processing style (Chaiken, 1987), or traits associated with valuing the benefits of internal processing, such as high need for autonomy or high need for competence (Vansteenkiste & Ryan, 2013), may lead individuals to place greater weight on internal processing benefits, reducing the likelihood of offloading.

text.text: Further, maximizers are more likely to leverage Gen-AI to synthesize large product sets, while satisficers use it for quick recommendations (Schwartz et al., 2002).

text.text: Privacy concerns and algorithm aversion reduce offloading propensity (Segijn et al., 2024), while positive past experiences amplify it (Gao et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Privacy concerns and algorithm aversion reduce offloading propensity <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Segijn et al., 2024)</ref>, while positive past experiences amplify it <ref type="bibr">(Gao et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The third category of moderators involves goals and performance priorities (Weis & Wiese, 2019).
text.formatted: The third category of moderators involves goals and performance priorities <ref type="bibr">(Weis & Wiese, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Past research has consistently found that performance goals of speed versus accuracy influence offloading strategy.
When accuracy is prioritized, individuals tend to offload more to external cognitive aids when those aids are perceived as reliable (Gilbert et al., 2020).
text.formatted: When accuracy is prioritized, individuals tend to offload more to external cognitive aids when those aids are perceived as reliable <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gilbert et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, when speed is prioritized, users offload less frequently, as relying on internal resources can sometimes be faster than the physical manipulation required to use a tool (Weis & Wiese, 2019).
text.formatted: By contrast, when speed is prioritized, users offload less frequently, as relying on internal resources can sometimes be faster than the physical manipulation required to use a tool <ref type="bibr">(Weis & Wiese, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Consumer goal orientation further shapes this propensity: consumers driven by utilitarian goals, those focused on efficient task completion, are more likely to delegate evaluative work to Gen-AI, whereas consumers motivated by experiential or hedonic goals, such as the enjoyment of browsing or identity expression through product discovery, derive value from the search process itself and are therefore less likely to offload (Hirschman & Holbrook, 1982).

text.text: This line of results suggests that offloading involves strategic planning based on one's goals.
Situational context constitutes a final category of moderators.

Time pressure and decision urgency increase offloading propensity by narrowing the window for internal deliberation and raising the relative cost of effortful internal processing-under time constraints, consumers adaptively shift toward faster, lower-effort strategies, including external delegation (Payne, Bettman, & Johnson, 1988).

text.text: Information environment complexity introduces a parallel pressure: when product landscapes are dense or option volumes are high, internal processing capacity is more readily exceeded, shifting the cost-benefit calculus toward external delegation (Malhotra, 1982).

text.text: The decision to offload to Gen-AI produces a range of cognitive and persuasive outcomes.
Prior research on cognitive offloading documents systematic effects on objective memory for offloaded content, metacognitive judgments, and decision performance.

Extending these findings to an advertising context, we examine how experimentally validated offloading effects translate into consumer and brand outcomes, including three interrelated clusters: (1) memory trade-offs and product learning, (2) metacognitive illusions that inflate cognitive self-esteem and decision confidence, and (3) post-offloading verification costs and their implications for decision quality (See online supplement, Table 2 for a complete list of propositions and conjectures).

text.text: The most robust finding in cognitive offload literature is that delegation to an external cognitive aid impairs memory for the offloaded content (Eskritt & Ma, 2014; Henkel, 2014; Grinschgl et al., 2021).

text.text: The resource redistribution process then produces an asymmetric memory profile: freed from encoding brand-level factual content, the consumer's available cognitive resources are directed toward the AI's evaluative outputs, including the summary judgment, the ranked recommendation, and the explanatory rationale, such that consumers encode what the AI concluded rather than the evidence from which that conclusion derives.
Proposition 1: Memory Trade-offs.
Compared to consumers who evaluate products internally, consumers who offload product evaluation to Gen-AI will show (a) lower recall of brand names and factual product attributes.
Within the offloading group, (b) consumers will recall AI-generated evaluative summaries better than they recall the brand attributes and product information underlying those summaries.
P1a and P1b are driven by two distinct sub-processes operating through different phases of cognitive resource reallocation.

P1a is driven by anticipatory encoding suppression: the expectation of continued AI access de-prioritizes internal encoding prospectively, before the AI response is received (Sparrow et al., 2011; Storm & Stone, 2015).

text.text: P1b is driven by active redistribution of freed resources: once suppression has reduced the encoding load for brandattribute content, released cognitive resources are directed toward the AI output that occupies the consumer's attention at delivery (Dupont et al., 2021; Gilbert, 2024; Storm & Stone, 2015).

text.text: The mechanism of anticipatory encoding suppression operates at Stages 1-5 of the delegation continuum, and the effect of memory impairment should increase as delegation level increases.
The memory impairment at Stage 1, storage and retrieval, is well-validated (Eskritt & Ma, 2014; Henkel, 2014).

At Stages 6-7 (Execution-Automated Action), brand knowledge deficits persist and worsen, but the causal pathway is non-exposure rather than suppression.
The memory effects predicted in Cluster 1 depend primarily on consumers' expectations of future AI accessibility.

Anticipatory encoding suppression should be strongest when consumers believe the delegated information will remain reliably accessible, because this expectation reduces the need to encode brand information internally.

Cognitive offloading has been shown to distort metacognition, which refers to individuals' awareness and understanding of their own knowledge (Risko & Gilbert, 2016).

text.text: Research suggests that relying on external tools can create illusions of knowledge: individuals experience feelings of being informed without actually carefully processing or understanding the underlying content, and misattribute the information available in the external cognitive aid to their own internal "in-thehead" knowledge (Fisher et al., 2015). Ward (2021) found that using Google to answer trivia questions inflated confidence in one's own memory and thinking, showing a misattribution of the search engine's retrieval to internal knowledge. Hamilton and Yao (2018) further showed that device ownership amplifies this boundary blurring, with participants using their own smartphones showing stronger metacognitive self-esteem inflation than those using a control device.

Rozenblit and Keil's (2002) study found that people tend to systematically overestimate how deeply they understand complex causal mechanisms, suggesting that misattribution of cognitive competence can operate across reasoning domains.

text.text: Yet the literature has not examined whether offloading evaluative reasoning to an external tool similarly inflates metacognitive selfassessments of one's own evaluative capacity.

This is what the current paper discusses: when consumers delegate not just information retrieval but also product evaluation to Gen-AI, their inflated metacognitive self-esteem may shift from memory and access confidence to decisionmaking confidence.
The conditions for this extended misattribution are more fully met in a Gen-AI-mediated decision-making context than in contexts mediated by any prior technology.

When Gen-AI synthesizes across sources, weighs trade-offs, performs product evaluation, and delivers a confident recommendation in a single seamless interaction, the boundary between internal and external processing becomes less transparent: consumers may feel that they are informed and have made well-thought-out decisions, without realizing that the bulk of the information processing actually took place within the Gen-AI system, rather than in their brain.
The proposed mechanism of this outcome is the cognitive illusion of agency.

Cognitive illusion of agency describes the process by which consumers misattribute evaluative cognitive work performed by an external system (e.g., Gen-AI) to their own internal cognition, mistaking access to AI-generated outputs for personal understanding (Fisher et al., 2015) and conflating externally sourced with internally held knowledge (Ward, 2021; Hamilton & Yao, 2018).

text.text: Two possible components contribute to this blurry boundary: source misattribution (Ward, 2021) and fluency-driven confidence inflation (Schwarz et al., 2021).

text.text: The form of the cognitive illusion of agency and the subdimensions of metacognitive self-esteem inflation differ depending on the delegation stage.
At
Stages 1-3 (information retrieval, synthesis, and comparison), the operative form is the illusion of memory.

Consumers misattribute AI's retrieval and comparison of brand attributes and product information to their own memory and access competence, inflating Memory CSE and Access CSE (Hamilton & Benjamin, 2019; Ward, 2013 Ward, , 2021)).

text.text: At Stages 4-5 (evaluation, recommendation), the operative form is evaluative misattribution: consumers misattribute AI's evaluative reasoning to their own judgment, inflating Thinking/Processing CSE in the domain of decision-making.
At Stages 6-7 (decision execution and automated action), however, the mechanism shifts from misattribution to agency displacement.
In that case, consumers' cognitive illusion of agency may decrease, or even disappear (Collier et al., 2025).

text.text: Proposition 2a: Metacognitive Self-esteem inflation in memory: Consumers who offload information retrieval and comparison to Gen-AI at early delegation stages (Stages 1-3) will report higher Memory CSE for brand attributes and product information and higher Access CSE for locating relevant product information than consumers who process this information internally.

Proposition 2b: Metacognitive Self-esteem inflation in thinking: Consumers who offload product evaluation and recommendation processing to Gen-AI at mid-to-advanced delegation stages (Stages 4-5) will report higher Thinking/Processing CSE in the domain of decision-making than consumers who evaluate products internally.
Inflated Thinking/Processing CSE (P2b) has downstream consequences for state-level decision confidence.
When consumers feel they are capable evaluators, they feel increased confidence in this specific decision.

Processing fluency serves as a second metacognitive cue for reliability and accuracy, influencing consumers' judgments of truth and confidence (Reber et al., 2010; Petrocelli & Whitmire, 2017; Schwarz et al., 2021).

text.text: Further, Gen-AI produces fluent and confident responses with few uncertainty signals (Kidd & Birhane, 2023; Zhou et al., 2024) and systematically validates users' existing positions through sycophantic outputs (Rathje et al., 2025).

text.text: As a result, consumers may mistake AI's apparent confidence for their own, and develop decision confidence from AI's apparent expertise, even when the evaluative work was performed externally by AI.
These metacognitive illusions can negatively impact advertising effectiveness.
Consumers who feel well-informed are more likely to defend their existing judgment and discount new information (Perloff, 2018).

text.text: Moreover, reduced information seeking allows consumers to bypass the extended search and consideration phases where advertising and SEO efforts traditionally exert influence.

Together, Propositions 2-4 create a closed epistemic loop: the same Gen-AI interaction that impairs brand memory (P1) also inflates decision confidence (P3) and suppresses the information seeking (P4) that would otherwise correct for that impairment.
Consumers have reduced their brand encoding, misattributed that confidence to their own evaluative competence, and foreclosed the possibility of engaging in additional search behaviors.
Perceived AI expertise should strengthen the cognitive illusion of agency because authoritative AI outputs are more readily misattributed to one's own evaluative competence (Sundar & Kim, 2019).

The memory trade-offs, CSE inflation, decision confidence, and reduced information seeking examined in Clusters 1 and 2 are produced by the process of offloading itself, either through cognitive resource reallocation or the cognitive illusion of agency, rather than by whether the output of Gen-AI is objectively accurate and reliable.

Consumers who receive a flawed AI recommendation experience the same metacognitive inflation as those who receive an accurate one, because the illusion operates at the level of how the output is processed, not what it contains.
The objective reliability of the Gen-AI output, however, is a new conditional variable in Cluster 3.

This conditionality produces three distinct scenarios: (1) when AI is reliable and the consumer does not verify, offloading yields decision-quality gains; (2) when AI is unreliable and the consumer does not verify, offloading yields quality losses, along with the inflated confidence and reduced information seeking from Cluster 2; and (3) when AI is unreliable and the consumer verifies, cognitive and emotional costs emerge, influencing consumer experience and brand evaluation.
These three scenarios guide Propositions 5, 6, and 7, and form the verification tradeoff that serves as the central tension in Cluster 3.
Cluster 3 does not introduce a new cognitive mechanism.
Instead, it focuses on delegation recalibration, where the original antecedent of offloading-the cost-benefit analysis of internal versus external processing-is reactivated.

When AI reliability does not meet consumers' expectations, consumers re-enter this decision process, weighing the expected utility of continued external processing against the costs and benefits of shifting back to internal processing (Gilbert, 2024).
text.formatted: When AI reliability does not meet consumers' expectations, consumers re-enter this decision process, weighing the expected utility of continued external processing against the costs and benefits of shifting back to internal processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Gilbert, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Because the recalibration operates at the level of the offloading decision itself (i.e., an antecedent of offloading), it is not treated as a new mechanism.
Under stable reliability, the offloading decision is made once and the consumer proceeds without re-evaluation.

When reliability is disrupted, such as when the system produces a noticeable error, consumers re-engage with the offloading decision and the delegation continuum, but with updated cost and benefit estimates.

In this case, the expected value of AI processing decreases, but the benefit of internal processing increases, making them less likely to offload or more likely to move back to earlier stages of the delegation continuum.
Past research supports this calibration dynamic (Weis & Wiese, 2019b; Gilbert et al., 2020).

text.text: When the tool is unreliable or performance falls below a certain threshold, users shift cognitive offloading behavior and retain more information internally.
and perform structured analyses that exceed individual cognitive capacity under real-world conditions.

When AI outputs are accurate, well-calibrated, and aligned with the consumer's evaluative goal, offloading to Gen-AI can produce objectively better decisions than consumers would reach through internal processing alone.

Empirical evidence from the cognitive offloading and decision-aid literatures shows that offloading to reliable external cognitive aids enhances accuracy and provides immediate performance gains across multiple cognitive tasks, including higher attentional accuracy (Wahn et al., 2023) and greater computational efficiency (Gao & Garagnani, 2025).

Cognitive costs of verification.

When AI outputs are uncertain, biased, or opaque, users may engage in verification behaviors, introducing additional cognitive costs that either pure offloading or pure internal evaluation would not have required.
Independent evaluation requires a single sequence of cognitive operations: the consumer assesses available information, weighs options, and chooses.

Verification of an AI recommendation requires a minimum of three: understanding AI's conclusion, independently evaluating its soundness, and resolving discrepancies between the AI's output and the consumer's own assessment.
Verifying AI-provided sources further adds to the cognitive burden.
Consumers need to determine whether the source exists, is relevant, and is accurately presented, a task that consumers who lack AI literacy often fail to perform efficiently (Rheu & Cho, 2025).

text.text: The increased cognitive cost generated by the subsequent recalibration is consistent with automation research showing that monitoring and verifying automated outputs increases mental workload relative to performing the task manually (Lyell & Coiera, 2017).

text.text: Therefore, when AI is unreliable and fails to meet consumers' needs, the additional steps may compound on top of initial evaluation work, making it more cognitively demanding than the single task of independent evaluation.
Beyond cognitive load, verification introduces emotional costs.

Consumers who discover during delegation that an AI recommendation was inaccurate or biased are likely to feel that a decision has been invalidated after they have already begun they have already begun to psychologically commit to, creating uncertainty and disrupting the confidence generated by the processing fluency (P3).
AI-mediated service failures consistently increase frustration, distress, and dissatisfaction (Castillo et al., 2021).

text.text: Worse, past research often observes a "spillover" effect, in which the emotional response of blame is frequently redirected toward the service firm or the brand (Leo & Huh, 2020).

text.text: In product evaluation contexts, such spillover is particularly consequential for brands.
Even when the brand had no control over the AI's output, consumers' negative emotional responses to AI failures likely reduce subsequent brand attitudes and behavioral intentions (Chen et al., 2026).

text.text: Proposition 6: Verification Costs.

Consumers who offload product evaluation to Gen-AI will report (a) higher perceived cognitive effort and (b) increased negative emotions (upset, frustration, dissatisfaction) when verifying AI recommendations, compared to the cognitive and emotional experience of consumers who evaluate products internally.

Despite the costs specified in P6, verification simultaneously re-engages cognitive processing that offloading had bypassed, creating a verification trade-off in which these added costs partially restore the core cognitive effects of offloading identified in Clusters 1 and 2.

During verification, consumers re-encounter brand names, product attributes, and competitive positioning, partially mitigating the memory impairment established in P1 (Henkel, 2014; Storm & Stone, 2015).

text.text: The active verification and the realization that AI's output is inconsistent may also reduce the inflated cognitive self-esteem of consumers and the inflated decision confidence produced by the cognitive illusion of agency (Dunn, 2010), attenuating P2 and P3.

text.text: As a result, although the verification process may feel frustrating and cognitively taxing, consumers develop a more accurate perception of their metacognitive self-esteem and ultimately make more informed decisions.
Proposition 7: Verification Trade-off.

Among consumers who offload product evaluation to Gen-AI, those who verify AI recommendations will report (a) mitigated memory impairment for brand and product information relative to non-verifiers, reflecting restored encoding engagement, and (b) lower decision confidence relative to non-verifiers, reflecting attenuation of the metacognitive self-esteem from Cluster 2, establishing verification as the mechanism through which offloading's dual cognitive costs can be partially corrected, at the expense of the costs specified in P6.
Objective AI reliability determines which propositions in Cluster 3 become operative.

Reliability failures have relatively minor consequences during information retrieval (Stages 1-3), become most consequential when evaluative reasoning is delegated (Stages 4-5), and become largely irreversible once AI autonomously executes decisions (Stages 6-7).
Trust primarily determines whether consumers initiate recalibration after encountering reliability failures.
Consumers with lower trust in AI reliability tend to calibrate more actively, detecting reliability issues before they become deeply committed to AI-generated conclusions (Hoff & Bashir, 2015).

text.text: AI literacy should facilitate efficient verification by helping consumers recognize reliability failures and evaluate AI outputs more effectively.

Consumers who are aware of Gen-AI's hallucination tendencies are more likely to detect reliability failures early and execute verification with lower incremental cognitive costs (Rheu & Cho, 2025), reducing the verification cost in P6.

text.text: Verification should be most likely for consequential purchasing decisions where the perceived benefits of independent evaluation outweigh its cognitive costs.

High-involvement or high-stakes purchases heighten sensitivity to reliability signals and increase the perceived benefit of internal recalibration, making voluntary verification more likely even when P3's inflated confidence works to suppress it.
Comparatively, low-involvement purchases are more likely to remain delegated.
Finally, willingness to expend cognitive effort (e.g., high need for cognition) should determine whether consumers complete verification and realize the corrective effects predicted in P7.

text.text: The previously mentioned short-term effects may accumulate as reliance on AI offloading becomes routine.

As Gen-AI becomes a habitual decision intermediary, the episodic cognitive consequences proposed in Clusters 1 and 2 may consolidate into more durable shifts in consumers' autonomy, competence, and brand relationships.
Concurrently, individual cognitive shifts may aggregate to reallocate brand loyalty toward AI platforms (Campbell, 2025).
text.formatted: Concurrently, individual cognitive shifts may aggregate to reallocate brand loyalty toward AI platforms <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Campbell, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In this section, we theorize long-term implications across three escalating levels: consumers' autonomy illusion, competence erosion, and loyalty reallocation from brands to AI platforms.

2 Importantly, unlike the formally testable propositions in Clusters 1-3, the theoretical extensions in this section assume that the short-term effects proposed in P1-P7 hold and that their effects accumulate reliably over time.
Rather than serving as formal predictions, the following are offered as theoretically grounded conjectures intended to motivate more longitudinal and field-based investigation.

Building on the mechanisms proposed in Clusters 1 and 2, the long-term trajectory of habitual offloading may consolidate into an autonomy illusion, a systematic overestimation of one's agency and control when these are externally scaffolded or algorithmically constrained (MacKay & DeVries, 2022; Ponce-Rojo et al., 2026).

text.text: Building on predictions from P1 to P3, frequent offloaders may feel capable and autonomous, believing they "can make these decisions", but at the same time, lack the internal knowledge and deliberative skills for autonomous choice.
Further, this elevated confidence reduces the likelihood of verification of offloaded output (P4), reinforcing reliance on Gen-AI and further suppressing internal deliberation.
Over time, this selfreinforcing dynamic may produce a progressive dissociation between perceived autonomy and objective capability, creating an autonomy illusion.

Consistent with this account, Shaw and Nave (2025) found that higher trust in AI and lower need for cognition predicted greater cognitive surrender across repeated decision trials, suggesting 2 The long-term consequences of cognitive offloading to Gen-AI systems that we trace through C8-C10 are likely to extend well beyond the individual level.

text.text: These consequences emerge from the joint structure of human cognition and the technological systems that consumers increasingly rely on.
Individual cognitive shifts aggregate across episodes and often across populations, into outcomes that shape the broader advertising-consumer ecosystem.

Bainbridge's (1983) classic work on the "ironies of automation" captures the central tension: as a control system becomes more capable, the human operator becomes more crucial at the moments when the system fails.

As such, when consumers offload evaluation to generative AI, potential atrophy in consumers' ability to evaluate outcomes becomes more salient when guidance from the AI system is unreliable, opaque, or absent.

Phenomena like loss of knowledge about one's own preferences, taste, and category expertise can be considered as population-scale instantiations of this dynamic, with outcomes that reflect a coupled interaction of human and AI systems rather than just reflecting changes in individual consumers in isolation.

Consequently, autonomy illusion can have long-term consequences: consumers believe they are capable of independent decisions without realizing their growing dependence on AI or their underinvestment in competence building (Lu, 2024).

text.text: Based on the accumulating logic from P1 and P4, the conjecture also predicts lower objective competence in the long term.
If the memory trade-off proposed in P1 holds, habitual offloaders develop familiarity with AI-generated summaries but not with the underlying brand attributes and product information.

Without frequent encoding and reasoning processes, consumers miss the opportunity to cultivate decision heuristics or category schemas that support competent autonomous choice (Hamilton & Benjamin, 2019).

text.text: The reduced information seeking (P4) further suppresses the corrective experience needed for accurate self-assessment. León-Domínguez (2024) found that pervasive AI chatbot use may impair higher-order executive functions, including problem-solving, suggesting that the dependency is not merely a knowledge gap but a functional one.

text.text: Therefore, consumers may have eroded objective competence while maintaining a high sense of autonomy, creating a wide gap between perceived and actual competence.
Consumers who more frequently offload product evaluation to generative AI will report (a) higher perceived autonomy while (b) demonstrating lower objective competence (e.g., lower decision quality).
Then, what happens when AI scaffolding is removed?
The inflated metacognitive selfesteem (P2) and decision confidence (P3) are context-dependent: driven by AI's fluency and misattribution effects, they require AI's presence.
When AI is removed, that belief has no basis, and the inflated self-assessments cannot transfer to an autonomous decision context.

Therefore, habitual offloaders' perceived competence and decision confidence may be deflated, potentially even lower than those who never offloaded, as the habit of internal deliberation has atrophied (Shaw & Nave, 2025).
text.formatted: Therefore, habitual offloaders' perceived competence and decision confidence may be deflated, potentially even lower than those who never offloaded, as the habit of internal deliberation has atrophied <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Shaw & Nave, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The memory trade-off (P1) compounds this metacognitive collapse and further affects consumers' perceived competence and decision confidence.
Consumers who habitually offloaded did not encode brand attributes and product information in the first place, and believe this information will be externally accessible.

Past research demonstrates the performance cost when access is removed: offloading boosts performance when tools are available but impairs recall when they are removed (Grinschgl et al., 2021; Richmond & Taylor, 2025).
text.formatted: Past research demonstrates the performance cost when access is removed: offloading boosts performance when tools are available but impairs recall when they are removed <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Grinschgl et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Richmond & Taylor, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The habitual offloader therefore has to work with two deficits: the inflated metacognitive self-esteem has no basis, and the knowledge that could have filled the gap was never encoded.
As a result, consumers are at risk of becoming less resilient decision-makers, with diminished perceived competence and confidence in their own judgment.

Consumers who more frequently offload product evaluation to generative AI will report (a) lower perceived competence and (b) lower decision confidence when forced to make product decisions without Gen-AI, compared to consumers who evaluate products internally.
The loyalty reallocation from brands to AI platforms theorized here follows from two distinct mechanisms established in Clusters 1 and 2.
First, when consumers encode AI's evaluative summaries but not brand attributes (P1), the cognitive prerequisites for brand awareness, associations, and loyalty are never accumulated (Aaker, 1996).
text.formatted: First, when consumers encode AI's evaluative summaries but not brand attributes (P1), the cognitive prerequisites for brand awareness, associations, and loyalty are never accumulated <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aaker, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Second, building on P2 and P3, the positive metacognitive experiences generated through AI interaction are tied to the AI platform rather than to the brands it recommends.
As discussed, these psychological inflations are contextdependent and experienced through AI interaction.

Over repeated episodes, loyalty accumulates around AI platforms rather than brands: consumers may remain indifferent to which brand AI recommends while remaining loyal to the platform itself (Orrù et al., 2023; Urban et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Over repeated episodes, loyalty accumulates around AI platforms rather than brands: consumers may remain indifferent to which brand AI recommends while remaining loyal to the platform itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Orrù et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Urban et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Consumers who more frequently offload product evaluation to generative AI will report higher attitudinal loyalty to AI platforms compared to specific product brands within categories.
If C10 holds, AI-mediated loyalty reallocation may weaken brand equity (Aaker, 1996).
text.formatted: If C10 holds, AI-mediated loyalty reallocation may weaken brand equity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aaker, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: When AI mediates product choice, consumers may not be exposed to enough brand-controlled touchpoints to establish distinctive brand associations.
Instead, brand equity may be shaped by AI's recommendation criteria and training data.

For instance, habitual offloaders may select products based on AI's recommendations (e.g., "it is the most cost-effective option"), with a shallow and instrumental understanding of the brand or products.
As a result, brands risk being homogenized by AI recommendations and losing the distinctiveness through which equity is traditionally built.
The threat to brand equity extends further to the advocacy stage.
Brand engagement theory suggests that advocacy depends on accumulated brand experience (Van Doorn et al., 2010; Maslowska et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Brand engagement theory suggests that advocacy depends on accumulated brand experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Van Doorn et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Maslowska et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: When consumers remember AI evaluations better than brand information, they may also share AI's evaluation rather than their own product knowledge.
As a result, wordof-mouth recommendations may shift away from brand-specific beliefs and experiences to AI's endorsement of the brand (e.g., "AI recommended it").

text.text: Offloading consumer decision-making to Gen-AI drives fundamental changes in advertising strategy.
When consumers delegate information search, comparison, evaluation, and even decision-making to Gen-AI, brands must adapt their advertising strategies to account for AI intermediaries.
For instance, as AI synthesizes multiple sources of information, consistent branded messages become more important than the persuasiveness of a single message.
In addition, to be more machine-readable, brand attributes need to be stated more explicitly rather than implied via aspirational imagery or emotional narratives.

Further, brands may also need to monitor online presence and increase visibility on credible platforms, as AI systems tend to assign greater weight to such sources when generating and citing information.

This emerging practice is formalized as Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), in which brands optimize not for ranking algorithms but for the citation and synthesis logic of large language models (Aggarwal et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This emerging practice is formalized as Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), in which brands optimize not for ranking algorithms but for the citation and synthesis logic of large language models <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aggarwal et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Where traditional SEO targets keyword relevance and link authority, GEO requires structuring product information in machine-readable formats, building presence on high-authority platforms that AI systems weigh heavily, and stating brand claims explicitly enough to survive AI summarization without distortion.

Empirically, incorporating authoritative citations, statistical evidence, and verifiable persuasive language meaningfully increases the likelihood of being cited in AI-generated recommendations (Aggarwal et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Empirically, incorporating authoritative citations, statistical evidence, and verifiable persuasive language meaningfully increases the likelihood of being cited in AI-generated recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aggarwal et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, such shifts also create risks.
When brand content is created to optimize for AI citation, brands may play the algorithm game rather than serve consumers' interests.
When brand content shifts from resonating with consumers to optimizing for algorithms, advertising risks losing creativity and authenticity.
These implications point to a broader tension: when AI-mediated consumer decisions press a brand to change how it communicates, such changes may weaken the consumer-brand relationship.
Ensuring that AI-mediated advertising serves consumer interests, rather than simply shifting power from brands to platforms, remains an open and pressing challenge.
Generative AI is rapidly becoming a central intermediary in consumer decision-making, fundamentally altering how information is accessed, evaluated, and acted upon.

This paper advances advertising theory by conceptualizing consumers' use of Gen-AI for product search and evaluation as a form of cognitive offloading, a value-based decision to delegate evaluative labor from the consumer to an external system.

By integrating insights from cognitive offloading, metacognition, and advertising research, we develop a unified framework that explains when consumers offload decisions to Gen-AI, how such offloading reshapes cognition and persuasion in the short term, and why its consequences extend to long-term consumer agency and brand equity.

In the short term, we suggest that offloading evaluation to Gen-AI produces systematic memory trade-offs, reallocating cognitive resources away from brand and product attributes toward AI-generated evaluative summaries.

This reallocation weakens traditional mechanisms of brand learning while fostering metacognitive illusions, including inflated subjective knowledge and decision confidence that dampen subsequent information seeking and reduce receptivity to advertising.
Although offloading can improve decision quality when AI is reliable, verification introduces cognitive and emotional costs while restoring knowledge accuracy.

In the long term, metacognitive illusions may develop into an autonomy illusion, a systematic mismatch between consumers' perceived agency and their actual decision competence, hindering consumers' competence and decision proficiency when autonomous decision-making is required without AI.
At the market level, memory trade-offs and AI-centered attribution shift evaluative equity away from brands and toward AI platforms, risking consumer loyalty and brand equity formation.
The paper concludes by identifying future research on calibrating AI reliance to preserve consumer agency.
Taken together, this work shifts the theoretical focus of advertising research from messages and exposures to the distribution of cognition in human-AI systems.
As evaluative judgment increasingly resides outside the consumer mind, core assumptions about learning, persuasion, and brand equity must be reconsidered.

By positioning cognitive offloading as the central mechanism linking generative AI to advertising outcomes, this paper provides a foundation for future advertising theory in an era of AI-mediated choice.

The offloading literature thus documents not a simple memory deficit but a systematic redistribution: what is encoded internally shifts from the delegated content to whatever information occupies the consumer's attention at the moment of resource availability.
Mechanisms.
Cognitive resource reallocation serves as a primary mechanism for the outcomes in Cluster 1.

Cognitive resource reallocation describes the process of delegating confidence in one's ability to retain information), Thinking/Processing CSE (confidence in one's capacity to reason and evaluate), and Access CSE (confidence in knowing where to locate information externally).

In the consumer product evaluation context, Memory CSE refers to confidence in one's ability to recall brand attributes and product information; Access CSE refers to confidence in one's ability to locate or retrieve relevant product information when needed; andThinking/Processing CSE refers to confidence in one's capacity to evaluate, compare, and form judgments about products -the cognitive work most directly implicated in consumer decisionmaking.

Research: Calibrating Offloading and Restoring Consumer AgencyRather than treating these outcomes as inevitable, future research should examine how offloading can be calibrated to balance efficiency gains with consumer learning, autonomy, and sustainable brand equity.
Future research can explore interventions that shape calibration in cognitive offloading.
One stream of inquiry concerns interventions that interrupt processing fluency.
Instead of presenting information with high certainty(Kidd & Birhane, 2023; Zhou et al., 2024), AI can estimate its confidence level and note information gaps.
text.formatted: Instead of presenting information with high certainty<ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Kidd & Birhane, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Zhou et al., 2024)</ref>, AI can estimate its confidence level and note information gaps.

text.text: For instance, when providing recommendations about nutritional supplements, AI can note that its recommendation is based on general nutritional guidelines and that it does not have access to consumers' specific health conditions or current medications.

Such fluency-disrupting interventions may reduce metacognitive illusion and prompt consumers to seek verification from external sources.Another line of inquiry can involve reducing the cost of verification.
Up to now, AI has attempted to support verification by providing sources.
However, sources may be fabricated, loosely related, outdated, or still require substantial human effort to assess relevance and correctness.
Future research could examine how alternative design strategies reduce the perceived and actual costs of verification.

For instance, does explainable AI-highlighting key assumptions and reasoning-shift consumers from surface-cue reliance to substantive logic evaluation, and when does lowering verification costs foster appropriate scrutiny versus reinforcing overreliance?
